factual_claims.text: Thirteen empty frames remain hanging in the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum after the 1990 theft.
On 18 March 1990 two men dressed as police officers were buzzed into the museum at about 1:24 a.m. by a guard.
Thirteen works including a Vermeer and two Rembrandts were taken in an 81-minute robbery, later valued by the FBI at about 500 million dollars.

Isabella Stewart Gardner's will requires that her collection's arrangement never be altered, and the museum offers a 10 million dollar reward.

segments.narration: Empty frames have hung in this Boston museum since 1990. Thirteen of them. The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum refuses to take them down.
March eighteenth, 1990. Two men in police uniforms rang the side door at 1:24 a.m. The guard buzzed them in.
Eighty-one minutes inside. They cut a Vermeer and two Rembrandts out of their frames and left with thirteen works worth half a billion dollars.
So why has nobody been arrested? The statute of limitations ran out in 1995. By 2015 the FBI said both thieves were already dead.
Isabella Gardner's will froze her collection exactly as she left it. So the frames stay empty, and a ten-million-dollar reward stays unclaimed.

research.summary: The largest unsolved art theft on record. Two men in police uniforms were admitted to the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston at 1:24 a.m. on 18 March 1990, subdued two guards and spent 81 minutes removing 13 works, among them Vermeer's The Concert, Rembrandt's The Storm on the Sea of Galilee, a Manet, five Degas sketches, a Chinese gu and a French Imperial Eagle finial. FBI valuations rose from 200 million dollars in 1990 to about 500 million by 2000. The statute of limitations expired in 1995; the FBI said in 2013 it had identified the thieves with high confidence and in 2015 that both were dead, and it has never named them. Isabella Stewart Gardner's will bars any change to the arrangement of her collection, so the emptied frames were left hanging. The museum's standing reward is 10 million dollars, doubled from 5 million in 2017, plus 100,000 dollars for the eagle finial.

segments.narration: A thousand American soldiers fought the war with inflatable tanks. The 23rd Headquarters Special Troops. Activated January 1944. Their job was to be seen.
Rubber tanks, rubber jeeps, rubber artillery. Crews could raise a whole armoured division in a few hours, then pack it into trucks by morning.
How do you fake an army after dark? With sound. Engine noise taped at Fort Knox, blasted from halftrack speakers, audible fifteen miles away.
They ran more than twenty of these shows across France, Luxembourg and Germany, pulling enemy fire toward empty fields while real divisions moved elsewhere.
And nobody could be told. The files stayed classified until 1996, and the surviving men only got their Congressional Gold Medal in March 2024.

research.summary: The 23rd Headquarters Special Troops, nicknamed the Ghost Army, was a US tactical deception unit of roughly 1,100 men (82 officers and 1,023 enlisted in some accounts) activated 20 January 1944 and modelled on British deception at El Alamein. The 603rd Camouflage Engineers handled visual deception with inflatable tanks, guns, jeeps and aircraft and could build dummy formations, bivouacs and airfields in a few hours; the 3132 Signal Service Company Special handled sonic deception, with recordings made at Fort Knox with Bell Labs engineers, played through halftrack-mounted amplifiers and audible up to 15 miles; the signal companies ran spoof radio traffic. The unit worked near Normandy, Brest, Luxembourg, the Hurtgen Forest and a major Rhine crossing, in more than 20 deception campaigns, returning to the US in July 1945. The operation stayed classified until 1996. President Biden signed the Ghost Army Congressional Gold Medal Act on 1 February 2022 and the medal was presented at the US Capitol on 21 March 2024.

factual_claims.text: When the H. L. Hunley was recovered, the remains of its eight crewmen were found seated at their stations, the submarine having been lost since 1864.
On 17 February 1864 the Hunley drove a spar torpedo into the USS Housatonic off Charleston, sinking it in about three minutes — the first warship sunk by a submarine.
The Hunley sank three times and 21 men died aboard it in total, eight of them in the third and final loss.
The wreck was located in 1995 and raised on 8 August 2000; the skeletons showed no trauma, the bilge pump was not set to clear water, and the keel release weights had never been released.
A 2017 Duke University study in PLOS ONE concluded the crew were most likely killed by the blast of their own 135-pound torpedo, detonated less than 16 feet from the bow.

segments.narration: Divers found the crew still seated at their stations. Eight men. Inside a Confederate submarine that had been missing on the seabed since 1864.
February 1864, off Charleston. The Hunley drove a spar torpedo into the USS Housatonic, sinking it in three minutes. History's first submarine kill.
Then it never came home. Twenty-one men died inside this boat across three separate sinkings. So what killed the final eight?
Located in 1995, raised in 2000. No skeleton showed injury. The pump was never set to clear water. Nobody had released the escape weights.
In 2017 Duke researchers named the likely killer: their own torpedo. A hundred and thirty-five pounds of powder, sixteen feet away. The blast wave went through the hull, and through them.

research.summary: The Confederate submarine H. L. Hunley sank three times, killing 21 men in all: five on 29 August 1863, eight on 15 October 1863 including Horace Hunley, and eight on 17 February 1864 after it drove a spar torpedo into the 1,240-ton USS Housatonic off Charleston, sinking it in about three minutes with five of her crew lost. Diver Ralph Wilbanks located the wreck in April 1995 on a NUMA expedition and it was raised on 8 August 2000. The remains were found seated at their stations with no skeletal trauma and no sign of an escape attempt; in 2008 researchers reported the bilge pump had not been set to clear the crew compartment, and in 2018 that the keel release blocks had never been released. A 2017 PLOS ONE study by Duke blast-trauma researchers led by Rachel Lance concluded the crew were most likely killed instantly by pulmonary blast trauma from their own 135-pound black-powder torpedo, detonated less than 16 feet from the bow, with individual survival odds under about 16 per cent. Naval History and Heritage Command archaeologists have disputed that conclusion.

factual_claims.text: Joshua Abraham Norton, a bankrupt San Francisco rice trader, issued his own currency and declared himself Emperor of the United States.

On 17 September 1859 Norton hand-delivered his proclamation to the San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin, which printed it that evening, and on 12 October 1859 he decreed the abolition of the US Congress.
Norton issued promissory notes in denominations from 50 cents to 10 dollars and some San Francisco businesses accepted them.
In 1867 a special officer arrested Norton for involuntary mental treatment, and after public outrage the police chief ordered his release and apologised.
Norton collapsed and died on 8 January 1880; about 10,000 people came to view his body, and he had decreed a bridge linking Oakland and San Francisco, built as the Bay Bridge in 1936.

segments.narration: He printed his own money and San Francisco spent it. Joshua Norton. A bankrupt rice trader who declared himself Emperor of the United States.
September 1859. He hand-delivered the proclamation to a newspaper, which printed it that same evening. Weeks later he abolished Congress by decree.
Congress ignored him. His city did not. Restaurants took his hand-made banknotes, fifty cents to ten dollars, as real currency.
Why would a whole city play along? In 1867 a guard arrested him as insane. The outrage was loud enough that the police chief apologised.
He died on a sidewalk in 1880, broke. Ten thousand people came to view the body — and the bay bridge he had decreed was finally built in 1936.

research.summary: Joshua Abraham Norton, probably born 1818 in England, was ruined speculating on rice in San Francisco. On 17 September 1859 he hand-delivered a letter declaring himself 'Emperor of these United States' to the San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin, which printed it that evening; on 12 October 1859 he decreed the abolition of the US Congress and in January 1860 ordered General Winfield Scott to clear its halls, which the Army and Congress ignored. He issued his own scrip in denominations of 50 cents to 10 dollars, accepted by some San Francisco restaurants (surviving notes now fetch over 10,000 dollars at auction), and received free meals, ferry and train passage. In 1867 special officer Armand Barbier arrested him for involuntary mental treatment; public outrage led Police Chief Patrick Crowley to release him with an apology. He issued decrees calling for a suspension bridge or tunnel linking Oakland and San Francisco, realised in the 1936 Bay Bridge and the Transbay Tube. He collapsed and died on 8 January 1880; about 10,000 people viewed his body before the funeral on 10 January. His remains were moved to Colma in 1934.

factual_claims.text: On Christmas Day 1950 four Scottish students removed the Stone of Scone from Westminster Abbey and it broke into two pieces; the stone weighs about 152 kilograms.
The stone was used to crown Scottish monarchs until Edward I of England seized it in 1296, after which English and British monarchs were crowned over it at Westminster.
The stone was taken to Scotland and left on the altar of Arbroath Abbey, where it was recovered on 11 April 1951.
The four students were identified but no charges were brought over the 1950 theft.
The stone was formally returned to Scotland on 30 November 1996, remains Crown property and is transported to London for coronations; since March 2024 it has been displayed at Perth Museum.

segments.narration: Four students stole the coronation stone and snapped it in two. Christmas morning, 1950. Westminster Abbey. A hundred and fifty kilos of sandstone.
Scottish kings were crowned on it until Edward the First seized it in 1296. After that, English and British monarchs were crowned over it.
They drove it north in pieces. Police hunted it for months. Then it turned up on an abbey altar in Arbroath.
So what happened to the four thieves? No charges. They were traced within months, and the Crown simply chose not to prosecute.
In 1996 Britain handed the stone back to Scotland, on condition it returns to London for every coronation. It now sits in a museum in Perth.

research.summary: The Stone of Scone, about 336 lb (152 kg), was used in the coronation of Scottish monarchs until Edward I seized it in 1296 and had it built into a chair at Westminster Abbey, after which English and British monarchs were crowned over it. On Christmas Day 1950 four Scottish students — Ian Hamilton, Kay Matheson, Gavin Vernon and Alan Stuart — removed it from the Abbey; it broke into two pieces during the removal. The larger part was buried in a field in Kent, then taken to Scotland and left on the altar of Arbroath Abbey, where it was recovered on 11 April 1951 and returned to Westminster about four months after the theft. The four were identified but no charges were brought; secondary accounts attribute this to a decision not to inflame Scottish nationalism. The UK government announced the stone's return to Scotland on 3 July 1996; it moved to Edinburgh Castle on 15 November 1996 with the official handover on St Andrew's Day, 30 November 1996. It remains Crown property and is taken to London for coronations, and since March 2024 it has been on permanent display at Perth Museum. The Westminster Stone theory holds that monks hid the real stone in 1296 and the English took a substitute.

factual_claims.text: On 27 November 1810 a stream of uninvited deliveries including wedding cakes, coal wagons and a coffin arrived at one London house whose occupant had ordered nothing.
The address was 54 Berners Street, home of Mrs Tottenham, and chimney sweeps began arriving at 5 a.m., followed by bakers with wedding cakes, furniture and an organ.
Police blocked both ends of Berners Street, and the Duke of Gloucester and the chairman of the Bank of England were among those who turned up.

Fifty-four Berners Street belonged to a Mrs Tottenham. Chimney sweeps knocked at five in the morning. Then bakers, furniture vans, an organ.
By afternoon police had to block the street. The Duke of Gloucester turned up. So did the chairman of the Bank of England.
Who does this to a stranger? A twenty-two-year-old writer named Theodore Hook, for a one-guinea bet that he could make any address famous.
He had spent six weeks writing up to four thousand letters. Police offered a reward and never caught him. He confessed in a novel, twenty-five years later.

research.summary: On 27 November 1810 the occupant of 54 Berners Street, Westminster — a Mrs Tottenham (sometimes spelled Tottingham) — was buried in uninvited callers and deliveries. Chimney sweeps arrived at 5 a.m., followed by dozens of coal wagons from the Paddington wharves, about a dozen bakers with wedding cakes, furniture, organs and a coffin; police blocked both ends of the street and a final wave of domestic servants expecting job interviews arrived at 5 p.m. Among the dignitaries drawn there were the Duke of Gloucester and the chairmen of the Bank of England and the East India Company; the Lord Mayor went on to the Marlborough Street magistrates to have police sent. The hoax was arranged by Theodore Hook, then 22, who had planned it from October 1810 with two accomplices and sent somewhere between one thousand and four thousand letters in Mrs Tottenham's name, for a one-guinea wager that he could make the address the most talked-about in London. A reward was offered and nobody was charged; Hook was suspected by 1812 and effectively confessed in his 1835 novel Gilbert Gurney.

research.summary: The Amber Room was begun in 1701 in Berlin, given to Peter the Great in 1716 and installed at the Catherine Palace at Tsarskoye Selo. Wikipedia's lead describes a room of more than 55 square metres holding over six tonnes of amber, with valuations from 142 million dollars (2007) to over 500 million (2016); the article's Architecture section gives a conflicting 450 kg figure for the panels. After Operation Barbarossa, Soviet curators failed to dismantle the brittle amber and Army Group North removed it within 36 hours; it reached Koenigsberg on 14 October 1941. In early 1944 it was crated into the castle basement. The RAF firebombed Koenigsberg in August 1944, Soviet artillery shelled the city, and it fell on 9 April 1945; documentation of the room's whereabouts ends at Koenigsberg. Soviet official Alexander Brusov concluded it was destroyed between 9 and 11 April 1945, a reading Scott-Clark and Levy support. Survival theories (a Mamerki bunker, the Wilhelm Gustloff, the SS Karlsruhe wreck found in 2020) remain unverified, and 1998 searches in Germany and Lithuania found nothing. The replica was approved in 1979, took 24 years and about 40 Russian and German experts, was helped by a 3.5 million dollar E.ON donation, and was dedicated in 2003.

factual_claims.text: In late 1726 Mary Toft, a clothier's wife from Godalming in Surrey, claimed to be giving birth to rabbits, and the case reached King George I's court.
Guildford surgeon John Howard delivered the specimens, a report of 19 November 1726 counted nine creatures, and the King sent his own surgeons including Cyriacus Ahlers.
Ahlers arrived on 20 November 1726, suspected a hoax, and found dung in one rabbit containing corn, hay and straw, which pointed away from a birth.
On 4 December 1726 Thomas Onslow discovered that Toft's husband had been buying young rabbits, and Toft confessed on 7 December 1726.
Toft's stated motives included fame and the hope of a royal pension; surgeon John Howard was fined 800 pounds on 7 January 1727 and Hogarth satirised the affair in a 1726 print.

segments.narration: Doctors told the King a woman was birthing rabbits. Godalming, Surrey, autumn 1726. Mary Toft, a clothier's wife, twenty-five years old.
A Guildford surgeon delivered nine of the creatures. London's medical elite came down to watch, and George the First sent his own surgeons.
One of them, Cyriacus Ahlers, examined a rabbit and found corn, hay and straw in its gut. A newborn had been eating hay?
On the fourth of December a nobleman found out Toft's husband had been buying young rabbits. She confessed three days later.
She had hoped for fame and a royal pension. Surgeon John Howard was fined eight hundred pounds, and Hogarth put the whole circus into a print.

research.summary: Mary Toft (nee Denyer, baptised 21 February 1703, died January 1763) of Godalming, Surrey, claimed from late October 1726 to be delivering rabbits and animal parts. Guildford surgeon and man-midwife John Howard delivered the specimens; Mist's Weekly Journal of 19 November 1726 counted nine creatures. Nathaniel St Andre, surgeon to the Royal Household, believed her; Henry Davenant visited on 4 November and Samuel Molyneux on 15 November. King George I sent Cyriacus Ahlers, who arrived on 20 November, suspected a hoax, found corn, hay and straw in a rabbit's dung, and reported to the king on 21 November. Richard Manningham brought Toft to London on 29 November, where she stopped producing rabbits under supervision. On 4 December Thomas Onslow, 2nd Baron Onslow, learned that Joshua Toft had been buying young rabbits, and a porter admitted being bribed to smuggle a rabbit in. Toft confessed on 7 December 1726 before Manningham and James Douglas, with further admissions on 8 and 9 December; secondary accounts add that Manningham's threat of a painful examination pushed her, and that she hoped for fame and a royal pension. She was held at Tothill Fields Bridewell, appeared at Westminster Quarter Sessions on 7 January 1727 and was discharged on 8 April 1727. Howard was fined 800 pounds on 7 January 1727; St Andre recanted on 9 December 1726; Hogarth satirised the case in Cunicularii (1726).

factual_claims.text: Excavations in Abu Qir Bay, about 7 km offshore and roughly 6 m deep, recovered around 70 ancient ships, described as the largest deposit of ships ever found in the ancient world.
The site is Thonis-Heracleion, Egypt's main port for international trade before Alexandria was founded in 331 BC, and finds include gold coins and a statue of Hapi holding four loaves.
A granodiorite stele carrying a decree of Nectanebo I confirmed the city's Egyptian name was Thonis, showing Thonis and Heracleion were the same place.

segments.narration: Divers found seventy ancient ships stacked in one bay. Abu Qir, east of Alexandria, seven kilometres offshore and six metres down.
This was Thonis-Heracleion, Egypt's gateway for foreign trade for centuries before Alexandria existed. Temples, gold coins, a statue holding four loaves of bread.
A granite slab carried a decree of Nectanebo the First and the city's real Egyptian name. So how does an entire port disappear?
The ground gave way. Around 101 BC heavy flooding liquefied the clay under the central island, and earthquakes and rising sea finished the job.
Franck Goddio's team located the city in 2000, after five years of searching the bay. He reckons about five percent has been excavated.

research.summary: Thonis-Heracleion was an ancient Egyptian port near the Canopic mouth of the Nile, about 32 km north-east of Alexandria, whose remains lie in Abu Qir Bay roughly 7 km offshore and about 5.8 m underwater. French underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio and his IEASM team, working with Egypt's antiquities ministry, located and excavated it after a five-year search; a stele found in 2000 showed Thonis and Heracleion were the same city. Finds include a granodiorite stele with a decree of Nectanebo I, about 70 ships (described as the largest deposit of ancient ships ever found), a baris Nile boat excavated 2009-2011, a 25 m Ptolemaic galley announced in August 2021, an intact statue of Hapi holding four loaves, gold and bronze coins, and a temple to Amun and Greek sanctuary to Aphrodite announced in September 2023. Activity peaked from the 6th to 4th centuries BC and Alexandria overtook it in the 2nd century BC. A major weather event, possibly a tsunami or earthquake, struck in the 2nd century BC; around 101 BC, probably after severe flooding, the ground under the central island succumbed to soil liquefaction, and earthquakes, tsunamis and rising sea level finished the city, which was under the sea by the end of the 8th century AD. Goddio estimates about 5 percent has been excavated.

factual_claims.text: Two wooden footlockers holding Peking Man fossils representing at least 40 individuals left Peking in 1941 and have never been recovered.
The fossils came from Zhoukoudian, known as Dragon Bone Hill, about 50 km south-west of Beijing, and in 1941 were to be sent to the United States for safekeeping.
US Marines were to carry the footlockers to the SS President Harrison at Qinhuangdao, but Japanese warships attacked the ship and it ran aground before reaching port.

segments.narration: Two crates of human fossils left Beijing and vanished. Inside were bones from at least forty individuals, dug out of a place called Dragon Bone Hill.
Zhoukoudian had produced the best early-human collection on earth. In 1941, with Japan closing in, China sent it to New York for safekeeping.
US Marines were to load the footlockers onto the liner President Harrison. The ship never made port. Japanese warships attacked it and ran it aground.
They left the medical college on the fourth of December, 1941, and were never reliably seen again. Sunk at sea? Ground up for medicine?
One marine said he dug up a box of bones at Qinhuangdao in 1947. A port researcher reckons the likely spot is under a parking lot.

research.summary: The Peking Man fossils were excavated from Zhoukoudian Locality 1, Dragon Bone Hill, about 50 km south-west of Beijing. The specimens shipped in 1941 represented at least 40 individuals and were packed into two wooden footlockers. By September 1941 Weng Wenhao and Raymond B. Fosdick had secured US embassy approval for the transfer; the US Marine Corps was to carry them from the Peking Union Medical College to the SS President Harrison, due to dock at Qinhuangdao, but the ship was attacked by Japanese warships and ran aground. The fossils left the college on 4 December 1941 and their whereabouts afterwards are unknown. Reports place them at Camp Holcomb, the Marine base at Qinhuangdao, when Japanese forces took it over on the morning of 8 December. Rumoured fates include loss aboard a sunken Japanese vessel such as the Awa Maru and being ground up for traditional medicine. Marine corporal Richard Bowen said he found a box of bones while digging a foxhole at Qinhuangdao in 1947; Wang Qingpu, author of a Chinese government report on the port, said that if Bowen's account is accurate the most probable location is under roads, a warehouse or a parking lot. Franz Weidenreich's casts, X-rays and notes went to the American Museum of Natural History in 1941, and four original teeth are held at Uppsala University.

factual_claims.text: On 30 May 1626 an explosion in Beijing threw a stone lion of about three tonnes over the city wall.
Everything within about 2 km was destroyed across roughly 4 square kilometres, the ground at the epicentre sank about 6.5 m, and large trees were thrown as far as Miyun.
Witnesses described a multicoloured, silk-like cloud compared to a black lingzhi mushroom that lingered over the site for hours.
The blast was centred on the Wanggongchang Armoury, one of six Ministry of Works gunpowder factories near Beijing, normally staffed by 70 to 80 people, and the death toll is put as high as 20,000.

There is no academic consensus on the cause; a gunpowder explosion is most commonly suspected, with a meteor airburst and a natural gas explosion also proposed, and the Tianqi Emperor's seven-month-old heir Zhu Cijiong died after the event.

segments.narration: A three-ton stone lion flew over Beijing's city wall. The thirtieth of May, 1626, mid-morning, in the reign of the Tianqi Emperor.
Everything inside two kilometres was gone. The ground at the centre dropped six metres, and full-grown trees came down out at Miyun, far outside the city.
Witnesses described a coloured cloud shaped like a black mushroom, hanging there for hours. What flattens a capital city in 1626?
The centre of it was the Wanggongchang armoury, one of six imperial gunpowder works, normally staffed by eighty people. As many as twenty thousand died.
Gunpowder is the obvious answer and still an unproven one. Historians have floated a meteor airburst too. The emperor's seven-month-old heir died after it.

research.summary: The Wanggongchang Explosion occurred in the late morning of 30 May 1626 in Beijing, about 3 km south-west of the Forbidden City in what is now Xicheng District, during the reign of the Tianqi Emperor. The Wanggongchang Armoury was one of six Ministry of Works gunpowder factories in the Beijing area and a main store of armour, firearms, ammunition and gunpowder for the Shenjiying capital defence force, normally staffed by 70 to 80 people. Possibly as many as 20,000 people died. Accounts describe a rumble moving north-east to south-west, a bright flash, destruction of everything within about 2 km across roughly 4 square kilometres, the ground at the epicentre sinking about 6.5 m, large trees thrown as far as Miyun, a roughly 3-tonne stone lion thrown over the city wall, tremors felt more than 150 km away, and a silk-like multicoloured cloud likened to a black lingzhi mushroom lingering for hours. Over 2,000 workers renovating Forbidden City palaces were thrown from roofs and died; Ministry of Works head Dong Kewei broke both arms; the emperor fled the Qianqing Palace, issued a repentance edict and 20,000 taels of gold for relief, and his only remaining heir, seven-month-old Crown Prince Zhu Cijiong, died from the shock. There is no academic consensus on the cause: a gunpowder explosion (mishandling, static discharge or sabotage) is most commonly suspected, with a meteor airburst, a natural gas explosion, a volcanic eruption and even a tornado proposed, and accounts may be exaggerated.

segments.narration: Lead coffins kept turning up jumbled inside a sealed tomb. Christ Church, Barbados. A stone door it took six men to shift.
The Chase family vault was opened in 1812, 1816 and 1819. Every time, the heavy coffins were somewhere other than where mourners left them. Who rearranges a tomb nobody can enter?
In 1819 the governor watched masons cement it shut. Sand on the floor, no footprints, no water marks. Opened in 1820: chaos again.

The whole legend traces to one account printed in 1833 and one unpublished note. Benjamin Radford checked the vault and found the brickwork undamaged.

research.summary: The Chase Vault is in the cemetery of Christ Church Parish Church, Oistins, Barbados. The story comes from an 1833 account by James Edward Alexander: Mrs Goddard was buried in 1807, Ann Maria Chase (aged 2) in 1808, Dorcas Chase (aged 12) in 1812, then their father Thomas Chase later in 1812; the vault was opened again in 1816 and 1819 and the lead coffins were reportedly found disturbed. The door was a massive stone requiring six or seven men to move, cemented shut by masons after each opening, and the sand floor reportedly showed no footprints or water marks. In 1819 Governor Lord Combermere was present and the coffins were found confusedly thrown about, some head down; a claimed account by Nathan Lucas describes a further opening in April 1820, after which the remains were reinterred separately and the vault left sealed and empty. The original account raised earthquake or flooding as possibilities without concluding. Andrew Lang (1907) found no support in the Christ Church burial register or contemporary Barbados newspapers, with only Lucas's unpublished account in support; Joe Nickell called the story historically dubious and suggested Masonic secret-vault symbolism shaped it, noting two named men were Freemasons; Benjamin Radford places it among moving-coffin legends, found no evidence of a deliberate hoax, and on inspecting the vault found the bricks intact with no damage consistent with heavy lead coffins moving. Skeptoid treats flooding and buoyancy as possible but unproven.

factual_claims.text: Archaeologists found tiny pools of liquid mercury about 17 m underground in a tunnel beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan, which was sealed around 200 CE.

The tunnel was discovered in late 2003 by INAH archaeologists Sergio Gomez Chavez and Julie Gazzola after heavy rain opened a sinkhole near the temple's base, and leads to a corridor nearly 100 m long.
The tunnel's walls and ceiling were coated with magnetite, pyrite and hematite, and it held a miniature mountain landscape with pools of liquid mercury representing lakes.
The identity of Teotihuacan's founders, their language and the city's original name are unknown, and the Nahuatl name Teotihuacan was given by the Aztecs centuries after the city fell.
Mercury is rare at ancient Mesoamerican sites and had not been found at Teotihuacan before; Sergio Gomez has suggested it represented an underworld river or lake and may point to a royal tomb nearby.

segments.narration: Pools of liquid mercury sat under a Mexican pyramid. Teotihuacan, north-east of Mexico City. Seventeen metres down, sealed for about eighteen centuries.
Heavy rain opened a sinkhole in 2003 beside the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Below it, a shaft, then a corridor almost a hundred metres long.
The walls were coated in pyrite and magnetite so the passage glittered. Someone built a miniature landscape down there, with mercury for lakes. Why bury a map of the underworld?
Nobody knows who these people were, what language they spoke, or what they called this city. The Aztecs named it centuries after it fell.
Mercury is vanishingly rare in Mesoamerica. Sergio Gomez thinks it stood for an underworld river, and that a royal tomb may be close.

research.summary: Teotihuacan, north-east of modern Mexico City, was built from about 100 BCE to 250 CE and was the largest city in the Americas at its peak, covering over 30 square kilometres around 450 CE with population estimates from about 100,000 to 250,000. The identity and origin of its founders are uncertain, the original name is unknown (Maya texts call it puh, Place of Reeds), and the Nahuatl name Teotihuacan was given by the Aztecs centuries after the city fell, by which time it was already in ruins and treated as a pilgrimage site. In late 2003 INAH archaeologists Sergio Gomez Chavez and Julie Gazzola found a tunnel after heavy rain opened a sinkhole near the base of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent: an entrance about 14 m deep reached by a nearly 5 m vertical shaft, leading to a corridor nearly 100 m long ending in underground galleries, believed sealed around 200 CE. Finds include a miniature mountain landscape 17 m underground with tiny pools of liquid mercury representing lakes, walls and ceiling coated in magnetite, pyrite and hematite, four greenstone statues, hundreds of jarosite-coated clay spheres and jade-and-quartz-inlaid wooden masks. The mercury was reported publicly in April 2015; mercury is rare in ancient Mesoamerica, found at only one Olmec and two Maya sites and never before at Teotihuacan, and Gomez suggests it symbolised an underworld river or lake, with some researchers reading it as a sign of a nearby royal tomb. The city's ruling-class structures were sacked and burned around 550 CE, with internal unrest and drought and famine linked to the 535-536 extreme weather events as the leading explanations.

factual_claims.text: On 13 September 1848 near Cavendish, Vermont, a tamping iron was driven through Phineas Gage's head, and he spoke within minutes and walked with little help.
Gage was a blasting foreman for the Rutland and Burlington Railroad, and the tamping iron was 3 feet 7 inches long, 1.25 inches across and weighed about 13.25 pounds.
Physician Edward H. Williams found Gage sitting in a chair outside his hotel about 30 minutes after the accident.
John Martyn Harlow took charge of Gage's treatment, including draining an abscess, and published the account in which friends said he was no longer Gage only in 1868, after Gage's death.
Gage worked as a long-distance stagecoach driver on the Valparaiso to Santiago route in Chile from 1852, and CT studies of his actual skull concluded only the left frontal lobe was damaged.

segments.narration: An iron rod went through his head and he walked. Cavendish, Vermont, the thirteenth of September, 1848. Three foot seven of solid iron.
Phineas Gage was packing blasting powder when the charge went off early. The rod weighed thirteen pounds and passed clean through his skull.
He was talking within minutes. A doctor found him sitting in a chair outside the hotel half an hour later. How is that survivable?
John Harlow treated him, drained an abscess, and twenty years on wrote that friends said he was no longer Gage. That line built a legend.
Gage drove stagecoaches across Chile for years. Scans of his actual skull show only the left frontal lobe was hit.

research.summary: On 13 September 1848, around 4:30 pm, while preparing a roadbed for the Rutland and Burlington Railroad south of Cavendish, Vermont, blasting foreman Phineas P. Gage was tamping blasting powder when the charge fired, driving the tamping iron up through his left face and frontal lobe. The iron was 1.25 inches in diameter, 3 feet 7 inches long and 13.25 pounds, a pointed, fairly smooth cylinder. Gage had brief convulsions, spoke within a few minutes, walked with little help and sat upright in an oxcart for the ride of about three quarters of a mile to his lodgings; physician Edward H. Williams found him in a chair outside the hotel about 30 minutes afterwards, and John Martyn Harlow took charge around 6 pm and treated him, including draining a later abscess. Gage lost his railroad job, was exhibited at Barnum's American Museum, and in 1852 went to Chile as a long-distance stagecoach driver on the Valparaiso to Santiago route; his health failed in mid-1859, seizures began in February 1860, and he died on 21 May 1860, aged 36, of status epilepticus. His skull and the tamping iron are at Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum, redeposited by Harlow in 1868. Harlow published the no-longer-Gage account only in 1868, after Gage's death; Malcolm Macmillan concluded the popular picture of Gage as a boastful, violent drifter is inconsistent with the facts, that he held two jobs from 1851 until shortly before his death, and that later accounts embellished his behaviour. CT studies of the actual skull by Ratiu et al. and Van Horn et al. concluded the left frontal lobe was damaged and the right was not, correcting a 1994 study based on a deformed cadaver skull.
